{{Short description|SIMD CPU instruction set}}
{{Technical|date=July 2019}}
'''SSE4''' ('''Streaming SIMD Extensions 4''') is a [[SIMD]] CPU [[instruction set]] used in the [[Intel]] [[Intel Core (microarchitecture)|Core microarchitecture]] and [[AMD K10|AMD K10 (K8L)]]. It was announced on September 27, 2006, at the Fall 2006 [[Intel Developer Forum]], with vague details in a [[white paper]];<ref name=":0">[http://www.intel.com/technology/architecture-silicon/sse4-instructions/index.htm Intel Streaming SIMD Extensions 4 (SSE4) Instruction Set Innovation] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090530090240/http://www.intel.com/technology/architecture-silicon/sse4-instructions/index.htm |date=May 30, 2009 }}, Intel.</ref> more precise details of 47 instructions became available at the Spring 2007 Intel Developer Forum in [[Beijing]], in the presentation.<ref>[https://intel.wingateweb.com/published/BMAS005/BMAS005_100Eng.pdf Tuning for Intel SSE4 for the 45nm Next Generation Intel Core Microarchitecture] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308153939/https://intel.wingateweb.com/published/BMAS005/BMAS005_100Eng.pdf |date=March 8, 2021 }}, Intel.</ref>  SSE4 extended the [[SSE3]] instruction set which was released in early 2004. All software using previous Intel SIMD instructions (ex. SSE3) are compatible with modern microprocessors supporting SSE4 instructions. All existing software continues to run correctly without modification on microprocessors that incorporate SSE4, as well as in the presence of existing and new applications that incorporate SSE4.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://software.intel.com/sites/default/files/m/8/b/8/D9156103.pdf |title=Intel SSE4 Programming Reference |access-date=December 26, 2014 |archive-date=February 15, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200215144900/https://software.intel.com/sites/default/files/m/8/b/8/D9156103.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

Like other previous generation CPU SIMD instruction sets, SSE4 supports up to 16 registers, each 128-bits wide which can load four 32-bit integers, four 32-bit single precision floating point numbers, or two 64-bit double precision floating point numbers.<ref name=":0" /> SIMD operations, such as vector element-wise addition/multiplication and vector scalar addition/multiplication, process multiple bytes of data in a single CPU instruction. SSE4.2 introduced new SIMD string operations, including an instruction to compare two string fragments of up to 16 bytes each.<ref name=":0" /> SSE4.2 is a subset of SSE4 and it was released a few years after the initial release of SSE4.

==SSE4 subsets==
Intel SSE4 consists of 54 instructions. A subset consisting of 47 instructions, referred to as ''SSE4.1'' in some Intel documentation, is available in [[Penryn (microarchitecture)|Penryn]]. Additionally, ''SSE4.2'', a second subset consisting of the seven remaining instructions, is first available in [[Nehalem (microarchitecture)|Nehalem]]-based [[Core i7]]. Intel credits feedback from developers as playing an important role in the development of the instruction set.

Starting with [[K10 (microarchitecture)|Barcelona]]-based processors, [[AMD]] introduced the ''SSE4a'' instruction set, which has four SSE4 instructions and four new SSE instructions. These instructions are not found in Intel's processors supporting SSE4.1 and AMD processors only started supporting Intel's SSE4.1 and SSE4.2 (the full SSE4 instruction set) in the [[Bulldozer (microarchitecture)|Bulldozer]]-based FX processors. With SSE4a the misaligned SSE feature was also introduced which meant unaligned load instructions were as fast as aligned versions on aligned addresses. It also allowed disabling the alignment check on non-load SSE operations accessing memory.<ref>{{cite web |title="Barcelona" Processor Feature: SSE Misaligned Access|url=http://developer.amd.com/community/blog/2008/04/14/barcelona-processor-feature-sse-misaligned-access/|publisher=AMD|access-date=March 3, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160809220231/http://developer.amd.com/community/blog/2008/04/14/barcelona-processor-feature-sse-misaligned-access/|archive-date=August 9, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> Intel later introduced similar speed improvements to unaligned SSE in their Nehalem processors, but did not introduce misaligned access by non-load SSE instructions until [[Advanced Vector Extensions|AVX]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Inside Intel Nehalem Microarchitecture|url=http://www.hardwaresecrets.com/article/Inside-Intel-Nehalem-Microarchitecture/535/7|access-date=March 3, 2015|archive-date=April 2, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402125657/http://www.hardwaresecrets.com/article/Inside-Intel-Nehalem-Microarchitecture/535/7|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Name confusion==
What is now known as [[SSSE3]] (Supplemental Streaming [[SIMD]] Extensions 3), introduced in the [[Intel Core 2]] processor line, was referred to as SSE4 by some media until Intel came up with the SSSE3 moniker. Internally dubbed Merom New Instructions, Intel originally did not plan to assign a special name to them, which was criticized by some journalists.<ref name="sse4criticism">[http://www.dailytech.com/article.aspx?newsid=3348 My Experience With "Conroe"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131015110825/http://www.dailytech.com/article.aspx?newsid=3348 |date=October 15, 2013 }}, DailyTech</ref> Intel eventually cleared up the confusion and reserved the SSE4 name for their next instruction set extension.<ref name="sse4newinstructions">[https://web.archive.org/web/20070106130924/http://download.intel.com:80/technology/architecture/new-instructions-paper.pdf Extending the World's Most Popular Processor Architecture] , Intel</ref>

Intel is using the marketing term ''HD Boost'' to refer to SSE4.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.intel.com/technology/product/demos/hdb/demo.htm|title=Intel - Data Center Solutions, IOT, and PC Innovation|work=Intel|access-date=September 17, 2009|archive-date=February 7, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130207023603/http://www.intel.com/technology/product/demos/hdb/demo.htm|url-status=live}}</ref>

==New instructions==
Unlike all previous iterations of SSE, SSE4 contains instructions that execute operations which are not specific to multimedia applications.  It features a number of instructions whose action is determined by a constant field and a set of instructions that take XMM0 as an implicit third operand.

Several of these instructions are enabled by the single-cycle shuffle engine in Penryn. (Shuffle operations reorder bytes within a register.)

===SSE4.1===
These instructions were introduced with [[Penryn (microarchitecture)|Penryn microarchitecture]], the 45&nbsp;nm shrink of Intel's [[Intel Core (microarchitecture)|Core microarchitecture]].  Support is indicated via the CPUID.01H:ECX.SSE41[Bit 19] flag.

| The INSERTPS and PINSR instructions read 8, 16 or 32 bits from an x86 register or memory location and inserts it into a field in the destination register given by an immediate operand. EXTRACTPS and PEXTR read a field from the source register and insert it into an x86 register or memory location.  For example, PEXTRD eax, [xmm0], 1; EXTRACTPS [addr+4*eax], xmm1, 1  stores the first field of xmm1 in the address given by the first field of xmm0.

| Packed sign/zero extension to wider types

| <code>PTEST</code>
| This is similar to the <code>TEST</code> instruction, in that it sets the [[Zero flag|Z flag]] to the result of an AND between its operands: ZF is set, if DEST AND SRC is equal to 0. Additionally it sets the C flag if (NOT DEST) AND SRC equals zero.
This is equivalent to setting the Z flag if none of the bits masked by SRC are set, and the C flag if all of the bits masked by SRC are set.
|-
| <code>PCMPEQQ</code>
| Quadword (64 bits) compare for equality
|-
| <code>PACKUSDW</code>
| Convert signed DWORDs into unsigned WORDs with saturation.
|-
| <code>MOVNTDQA</code>
| Efficient read from write-combining memory area into SSE register; this is useful for retrieving results from peripherals attached to the memory bus.

===SSE4.2===
SSE4.2 added STTNI (String and Text New Instructions),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://software.intel.com/en-us/articles/schema-validation-with-intel-streaming-simd-extensions-4-intel-sse4/|title=Schema Validation with Intel Streaming SIMD Extensions 4 (Intel SSE4)|access-date=February 6, 2012|archive-date=June 17, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180617065748/https://software.intel.com/en-us/articles/schema-validation-with-intel-streaming-simd-extensions-4-intel-sse4/|url-status=live}}</ref> several new instructions that perform character searches and comparison on two operands of 16 bytes at a time.  These were designed (among other things) to speed up the parsing of [[XML]] documents.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://software.intel.com/en-us/articles/xml-parsing-accelerator-with-intel-streaming-simd-extensions-4-intel-sse4/|title=XML Parsing Accelerator with Intel Streaming SIMD Extensions 4 (Intel SSE4)|access-date=February 6, 2012|archive-date=June 17, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180617042918/https://software.intel.com/en-us/articles/xml-parsing-accelerator-with-intel-streaming-simd-extensions-4-intel-sse4/|url-status=live}}</ref>  It also added a <code>CRC32</code> instruction to compute [[cyclic redundancy check]]s as used in certain data transfer protocols. These instructions were first implemented in the [[Nehalem (microarchitecture)|Nehalem]]-based [[Intel Core i7]] product line, and complete the SSE4 instruction set. AMD on the other hand first added support starting with the [[Bulldozer (microarchitecture)|Bulldozer microarchitecture]]. Microsoft's [[Windows 7]] was the first operating system to implement SSE4.2, as support is indicated via the CPUID.01H:ECX.SSE42[Bit 20] flag.

[[Windows 11, version 24H2|Windows 11 24H2]] and [[Windows Server 2025]] require the CPU to support SSE4.2, otherwise the Windows kernel is unbootable.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Klotz|first=Aaron|date=2024-04-24|title=Microsoft blocks some PCs from Windows 11 24H2 — CPU must support SSE4.2 or the OS will not boot|url=https://www.tomshardware.com/software/windows/microsoft-updates-windows-11-24h2-requirements-cpu-must-support-sse42-or-the-os-will-not-boot|access-date=2024-04-29|website=[[Tom's Hardware]]}}</ref>

===<code>POPCNT</code> and <code>LZCNT</code>===
These instructions operate on integer rather than SSE registers, because they are not SIMD instructions, but appear at the same time and although introduced by AMD with the SSE4a instruction set, they are counted as separate extensions with their own dedicated CPUID bits to indicate support. Intel implements <code>POPCNT</code> beginning with the [[Nehalem (microarchitecture)|Nehalem]] microarchitecture and <code>LZCNT</code> beginning with the [[Haswell (microarchitecture)|Haswell]] microarchitecture. AMD implements both, beginning with the [[AMD K10#Characteristics of the microarchitecture|Barcelona microarchitecture]].

AMD calls this pair of instructions [[Bit Manipulation Instruction Sets|''Advanced Bit Manipulation'' (ABM)]].

The encoding of <code>LZCNT</code> takes the same encoding path as the encoding of the <code>BSR</code> (bit scan reverse) instruction. This results in an issue where <code>LZCNT</code> called on some CPUs not supporting it, such as Intel CPUs prior to Haswell, may incorrectly execute the <code>BSR</code> operation instead of raising an ''invalid instruction'' exception. This is an issue as the result values of <code>LZCNT</code> and <code>BSR</code> are different.

Trailing zeros can be counted using the <code>BSF</code> (bit scan forward) or <code>TZCNT</code> instructions.

[[Windows 11, version 24H2|Windows 11 24H2]] and [[Windows Server 2025]] require the CPU to support <code>POPCNT</code>, otherwise the Windows kernel is unbootable.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sen |first=Sayan |date=2024-03-17 |title=Microsoft fixes a misfired PopCnt block but Windows 11 24H2 requirements may be here to stay |url=https://www.neowin.net/news/microsoft-fixes-a-misfired-popcnt-block-but-windows-11-24h2-requirements-may-be-here-to-stay/ |access-date=2024-03-17 |website=[[Neowin]] |language=en}}</ref>

===SSE4a===
The SSE4a instruction group was introduced in AMD's [[AMD K10#Characteristics of the microarchitecture|Barcelona microarchitecture]].  These instructions are not available in Intel processors.  Support is indicated via the CPUID.80000001H:ECX.SSE4A[Bit 6] flag.<ref name="amd_cpuid"/>
